findings.issue_text: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up emails case-sensitively, so blocking can be bypassed by varying case; emails should be normalized (downcased) before lookup/storage with case-insensitive uniqueness
BlockedEmail match_count uses a read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) that loses updates under concurrent validation attempts; should use an atomic SQL update or optimistic locking

should_block? has side effects (DB writes) and is invoked from model validation, causing match_count/last_match_at to be incremented multiple times and saves during checks when validation runs multiple times in a save cycle; statistics and blocking checks should be separated

validates :email with if: :email_changed? skips the blocked/whitelist check entirely when the email hasn't changed, allowing the blocklist enforcement to be silently bypassed; consider on: :create or validating the blocklist check unconditionally
Validator performs no format/syntax validation of the email address itself despite claims of comprehensive validation
No specs covering the whitelist/blacklist branches of the new validator, nor that the composed validates :email behaves as the old validator did

Endpoint response shape changes: user.errors.to_hash exposes full error messages and values may reflect stale/case-folded attributes; added fields should be intentional and a client-side spec for the response shape is missing

Client-side rejectedEmails matches email with exact string comparison, so case changes or trailing whitespace get a fresh server round-trip instead of immediate rejection; trimming/normalizing before storing/comparing would align client and server
No controller/request spec for UsersController#create covering the new errors/values fields, and no client-side spec for the rejectedEmails behavior

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: validates :email with if: :email_changed? skips the blocked/whitelist check entirely when the email hasn't changed, allowing the blocklist enforcement to be silently bypassed; consider on: :create or validating the blocklist check unconditionally

adjudication.rationale: In `User`, the email domain/blocked-email logic is now in the custom validator and is still gated by `if: :email_changed?` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). That condition does not bypass checks on create (a new record’s email is changed from `nil`, so it will run). It also prevents changing an email to a blocked/forbidden one without triggering validation, since changing the value sets `email_changed?`. The finding’s “silently bypassed” implication isn’t supported by the diff; it’s at most a design choice about whether existing users should be revalidated when their email hasn’t changed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Validator performs no format/syntax validation of the email address itself despite claims of comprehensive validation

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, the new `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) only enforces domain whitelist/blacklist rules and `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, and does not check email syntax/format. Since `User` now uses `validates :email, email: true` (app/models/user.rb), a reviewer could reasonably flag that the custom validator named `EmailValidator` doesn’t actually validate email format. The part about “claims of comprehensive validation” isn’t evidenced in the diff, so this is more about misleading/incomplete validation scope than a clearly introduced defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No specs covering the whitelist/blacklist branches of the new validator, nor that the composed validates :email behaves as the old validator did

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `EmailValidator` with additional branches for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` and `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and changes `User` from a custom `email_validator` method to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` plus presence/uniqueness (app/models/user.rb). However, the added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` path and does not cover the whitelist/blacklist branches or assert that the new composed validations on `User` preserve the old behavior. This is a concrete, diff-grounded testing gap rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Endpoint response shape changes: user.errors.to_hash exposes full error messages and values may reflect stale/case-folded attributes; added fields should be intentional and a client-side spec for the response shape is missing

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes `UsersController#create` failure JSON from just `{success, message}` to also include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")`, which is an API/response-shape change that should be intentional and versioned/covered. The frontend now depends on this new shape (`result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` in `create_account_controller.js`) to populate `rejectedEmails`, but the diff adds no client-side contract/spec for the response structure. The note about `values` potentially reflecting normalized attributes is plausible given it uses `user.attributes` rather than the raw submitted params, but the exact staleness/case-folding behavior isn’t fully verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side rejectedEmails matches email with exact string comparison, so case changes or trailing whitespace get a fresh server round-trip instead of immediate rejection; trimming/normalizing before storing/comparing would align client and server

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` and checks `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email = this.get('accountEmail')`, and pushes `result.values.email` into the array on failure. This is an exact string comparison with no trimming or case normalization shown, so entering the same rejected address with different casing or trailing/leading whitespace would bypass the client-side rejection and trigger another server request. This doesn’t break correctness (server-side validation still runs) but is a concrete edge-case/performance/UX gap introduced by the new optimization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No controller/request spec for UsersController#create covering the new errors/values fields, and no client-side spec for the rejectedEmails behavior

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new behavior that is not covered by specs shown here: UsersController#create now renders additional JSON fields on failure (`errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`), but no controller/request spec is added in this PR to assert that contract. On the client, `create_account_controller.js` introduces `rejectedEmails` state and uses it to fail validation and to push rejected emails on create failure, but no client-side test/spec is added for this new caching/validation behavior. This is a concrete missing-test gap for newly added logic/API surface rather than a proven runtime defect.
